stack_and_runtime_constraints: TypeScript monorepo with root app code and AWS CDK stack.
Runtime is AWS serverless on Node.js 20.
Current orchestration is EventBridge Scheduler -> Producer Lambda -> SQS FIFO -> Orchestrator Lambda -> Step Functions -> Consumer Lambda.
Current persistence is DynamoDB with separate tables for pending records, idempotency, and results.
architecture_shape: Phase 2 already established provider isolation, operational lifecycle, retries, and idempotency.
The current producer model reads pending records and dispatches work items for a target date.
The current scope does not yet solve defendable processing of 1M+ pending records or temporal distribution at that scale.
likely_touched_modules: Producer dispatch flow and its record-selection strategy.
CDK infrastructure for large-scale scheduling, batching, or distributed execution.
Pending-record access patterns and partition-aware querying.
Phase docs and specs for operator validation at scale.
test_setup_available: TypeScript build with composite project references.
Jest unit tests for CDK, orchestrator, consumer, and adapters.
Manual AWS validation flow already documented for phase 2.

product_scope.problem_statement: The current system can process provider work items with resilience and operational control, but it still assumes a manageable pending-record volume. The challenge requires a defendable strategy for 1M+ records, distributed execution over time, and avoidance of monolithic scans or concentrated load against infrastructure and providers.
product_scope.goal: Extend the validated phase-2 flow with a functional strategy for massive-scale selection, distribution, and dispatch of work items so the architecture can defend daily processing of 1M+ records without abandoning provider isolation or operational control.
success_outcomes: The system no longer depends on a monolithic read of all pending records for a day.
Daily work can be distributed into smaller execution units that are operationally reasonable at 1M+ scale.
Dispatch pressure is spread in time and volume rather than concentrated in one execution burst.
Same-provider serialization remains intact while large-scale throughput is introduced.
The phase provides a defendable position on whether shuffle-sharding is adopted now, deferred, or explicitly rejected.

in_scope: Functional strategy for processing 1M+ pending records.
Functional decomposition of daily pending work into smaller execution units.
Temporal distribution of dispatch work to avoid a single concentrated burst.
Preservation of provider isolation while large-scale processing is introduced.
Explicit decision point on shuffle-sharding as part of the scalability story.
Functional expectations for operator reasoning about large-scale progress.
out_of_scope: Low-level implementation details of AWS-specific partitioning or pagination APIs.
Final cost tuning or exact throughput sizing.
Advanced observability dashboards and SLO programs.
Business-rule changes for provider classification or phase-2 lifecycle semantics.

actors.name: Scheduler Layer
actors.description: Starts or coordinates the daily processing windows.

actors.name: Mass Dispatch Flow
actors.description: Selects eligible records in scalable chunks and publishes downstream work.

actors.name: Operational Orchestration Flow
actors.description: Continues to own retries, idempotency, lifecycle, and final closure once a work item is dispatched.

actors.name: Provider Boundary
actors.description: Must continue receiving serialized requests per provider even when global throughput rises.

actors.name: Technical Reviewer
actors.description: Needs a defendable scale strategy for 1M+ records and a clear stance on temporal distribution and shuffle-sharding.

user_journeys.name: Daily workload is decomposed into scalable units
steps: The system identifies that a very large set of pending records is eligible.
The system breaks that workload into smaller dispatch units instead of attempting one monolithic read-and-send execution.
Those units are processed progressively until the eligible work for the day is exhausted.

user_journeys.name: Large-scale dispatch remains distributed over time
steps: A high-volume day requires many work items to be dispatched.
The system spreads that dispatch work over a reasonable temporal window instead of sending everything in one burst.
Providers continue receiving requests in an orderly way while overall progress continues.

user_journeys.name: Provider isolation survives global scale-up
steps: Multiple providers have eligible work at the same time.
The system increases global throughput for the daily workload.
Each provider still receives serialized work in order while different providers can progress independently.

user_journeys.name: Scale design is technically defendable
steps: A reviewer inspects the phase-3 design.
They identify the strategy for breaking up large pending workloads.
They understand how temporal spreading works and whether shuffle-sharding is part of the phase.
They can defend why the design is safer than a single giant scan and burst dispatch.

use_cases.title: Process a very large daily backlog
use_cases.description: The system must handle daily eligible work in the million-plus range without requiring one monolithic execution.

use_cases.title: Distribute dispatch over time
use_cases.description: The system must avoid concentrating all dispatch traffic into one narrow burst.

use_cases.title: Preserve same-provider ordering at scale
use_cases.description: The system must continue protecting providers from concurrency violations even while global throughput increases.

use_cases.title: Choose a defendable sharding posture
use_cases.description: The system design must explicitly state whether shuffle-sharding is adopted, deferred, or rejected for this phase.

use_cases.title: Keep phase-2 operational guarantees intact
use_cases.description: Scale behavior must not invalidate the idempotency, retry, and lifecycle guarantees already established.

business_rules.rule: The system must not depend on a single monolithic read of the entire daily pending workload.
Daily eligible work must be decomposed into smaller execution units that can progress independently.
Dispatch work must be spread in time or batches to avoid one concentrated burst against infrastructure or providers.
Same-provider serialization remains mandatory even when large-scale throughput is introduced.
Cross-provider progress may continue in parallel.
Phase 3 must preserve phase-2 resilience and idempotency guarantees rather than replacing them.
The phase must explicitly document its stance on shuffle-sharding as part of the scale strategy.
This phase prioritizes defendable scale behavior over final optimization, dashboards, or presentation tooling.

functional_requirements.title: Scalable pending selection
functional_requirements.statement: The system must support a scalable way to select daily eligible pending work without relying on one monolithic read.

functional_requirements.title: Workload decomposition
functional_requirements.statement: The system must decompose a very large daily workload into smaller dispatch units that can be processed progressively.

functional_requirements.title: Temporal distribution
functional_requirements.statement: The system must distribute dispatch work over time rather than issuing all work in one concentrated burst.

functional_requirements.title: Provider isolation preservation
functional_requirements.statement: The system must preserve same-provider serialization while enabling large-scale global progress.

functional_requirements.title: Cross-provider parallel progress
functional_requirements.statement: The system must continue allowing work from different providers to progress independently.

functional_requirements.title: Scale strategy traceability
functional_requirements.statement: The phase must make the large-scale selection and distribution strategy understandable to a technical reviewer.

functional_requirements.title: Shuffle-sharding decision
functional_requirements.statement: The phase must explicitly state whether shuffle-sharding is part of the current solution and why.

functional_requirements.title: Operational guarantee preservation
functional_requirements.statement: The phase must preserve the operational semantics established in phase 2 once work items have been dispatched.

interaction_expectations.expectation: A reviewer should be able to understand how the system avoids a giant one-shot daily scan and dispatch.
The scale model should feel like an extension of the existing architecture rather than a contradictory redesign.
The phase should leave clear room for later observability and cost-tuning work without requiring them now.

acceptance_criteria.given: A daily workload contains 1M+ eligible records
acceptance_criteria.then: The system does not rely on a single monolithic read-and-dispatch execution.

acceptance_criteria.given: A very large eligible workload exists for one day
acceptance_criteria.then: The workload is broken into smaller units that can progress progressively.

acceptance_criteria.given: The system has many work items to dispatch
acceptance_criteria.then: Dispatch is spread over time or equivalent distributed execution windows rather than one concentrated burst.

acceptance_criteria.given: Many work items belong to the same provider
acceptance_criteria.then: The provider still receives serialized processing in order.

acceptance_criteria.given: Work items belong to different providers
acceptance_criteria.then: The system may progress them independently in parallel.

acceptance_criteria.given: A reviewer examines the phase-3 design
acceptance_criteria.then: They can explain how the architecture handles 1M+ scale and why it is safer than a monolithic daily dispatch.

acceptance_criteria.given: A reviewer examines the sharding strategy
acceptance_criteria.then: They can see an explicit decision on shuffle-sharding and its role in the current phase.

acceptance_criteria.given: Phase-2 operational controls are already in place
acceptance_criteria.then: The scale strategy does not remove or contradict retries, idempotency, or lifecycle closure after dispatch.

assumptions: Phase 2 is the operational base and remains valid after phase-3 scale changes.
The business requirement is to defend a scalable architecture for 1M+ daily records, not necessarily to optimize every cost dimension in this phase.
Temporal distribution may be achieved through one or more orchestrated windows rather than a single daily burst.
Detailed selection mechanics, partitioning, and AWS service choices belong to the technical spec, not to this functional spec.

open_questions.question: Should phase 3 commit to shuffle-sharding in the first implementation, or only require a defendable decision with the option to defer it?
open_questions.resolved_as: Defer manual shuffle-sharding. Use Amazon SQS FIFO High Throughput mode and rely on automatic partitioning by MessageGroupId hash as the defendable scale posture for this phase.

open_questions.question: Should temporal distribution be treated as mandatory per-provider scheduling windows, or is distributed batch dispatch across the day sufficient for this phase?
open_questions.resolved_as: Use distributed batch dispatch across the day. EventBridge Scheduler will invoke dispatch work continuously across a 24-hour window instead of one monolithic daily burst.
